new_statements.quote: Una palabra fonémica (grupo acentual) en este dialecto del Orejón, generalmente se marca con el acento primario inicial en la raíz gramatical (la raíz siempre es inicial en una palabra fonológica). Este acento primario se encuentra en todas las sílabas de la raíz si las sílabas tienen tonos idénticos. Pero si los tonos no son idénticos, solamente las sílabas de tono alto se acentúan. Todas las raíces monosilábicas tienen el acento primario. [...] Los acentos primario y secundario, iniciales en una palabra fonológica, son de esta manera fonémicos, ya que su ubicación es predecible sólo gramaticalmente, aunque no estén escritos en este trabajo. [p. 9, sec. 2.1.1:] Hay dos tonos contrastivos en el Orejón: alto /´/ y bajo / / (no diacrítico).
new_statements.translation: A phonemic word (accentual group) in this dialect of Orejón is generally marked with primary accent initial on the grammatical root (the root is always initial in a phonological word). This primary accent is found on all syllables of the root if the syllables have identical tones. But if the tones are not identical, only the high-tone syllables are accented. All monosyllabic roots carry primary accent. [...] The primary and secondary accents, initial in a phonological word, are in this way phonemic, since their location is predictable only grammatically, although they are not written in this work. [p. 9:] There are two contrastive tones in Orejón: high /´/ and low (no diacritic).

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for orej1242 has an empty rule and there are no existing statements; this source supplies the first placement statement: a two-tone language with grammatically predictable root(-initial) primary accent conditioned by root tone, plus rhythmic secondary accent on suffixes. Nothing in the catalog is contradicted.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Orejón has two contrastive lexical tones (high, low), demonstrated with minimal pairs and root tone patterns (HH, HL, LL; LHL, HHL, HLL, LLL on trisyllables). Word accent is separate from tone and morphologically placed: primary accent falls on the root, which is always word-initial; within a polysyllabic root every syllable is accented if the root's tones are all identical, otherwise only the high-toned root syllables are accented; monosyllabic roots always bear primary accent. Accent placement is predictable from grammatical structure (root position), not lexically contrastive, and the authors do not write it. Intonation starts high and declines through the phonological word; word boundaries are cued by primary accent plus a pitch reset.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary accent falls on the first syllable of a polysyllabic suffix string immediately after the root and then on alternate syllables of the following suffixes in a regular predictable pattern (examples /ʔi"hína?/ 'todos los gusanos', /hĩgo"húna?/ 'todas las palomas', with " marking secondary accent); it weakens progressively toward the end of the phonological word. Footnote 7 adds morphotonemic rules: all suffixes are underlyingly low; the first syllable of a suffix string becomes high; if the string has only two syllables the second is also high when open; a single monosyllabic suffix copies the tone of the root-final syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Roots with non-identical tones: only the high-toned syllables take primary accent (so an LH(L) root has non-initial primary accent within the root). Four-syllable forms are compounds of two or more roots and 'there may be other primary accents inside the word'. Contrastive interrogative intonation patterns noted but deferred to a future grammar. Description is of the Esperanza (Loreto) dialect, ~50 speakers; Sucusari, Yanayacu and Algodón river dialect variants are mentioned only for segmental allophony ([tš] of /s/, [gw]~[ʔu], [y]~[dž]), not for accent.
new_statements.identity_note: Velie, Brend & Powlison 1976 describe the Orejón dialect spoken by about fifty people at Esperanza, Loreto, Peru (data collected by Velie 1958-1960); variants from the Sucusari, Yanayacu and Algodón river dialects are cited only for segmental allophones. The language is the one now called Máíhɨ̃kì/Maihiki (orej1242); the paper uses the exonym Orejón (also 'coto' in the 1975 title).

readall_conflicts: No new source was opened, so no new disagreement can be established. The only known tension is second-hand: the two SIL works (Velie 1975: 12-13; Velie et al. 1976: 11-12) speak of 'acento' in Orejón, which the catalog's deciding source (Farmer & Michael 2013 ms, fn. 19, p. 35) judges 'does not correspond to the modern understanding of stress'; whether the SIL 'acento' is a stress rule (e.g. a fixed-position prominence) or a notation for the H tone cannot be checked until SIL entry 30074) or the DEL 10 sketch is obtained through a browser or a library.

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: The 'tonal, no word stress' coding rests on the two best available first-hand descriptions: Farmer's 2015 Berkeley dissertation (phonology chapter, all three dialects) and the dedicated Farmer & Michael 2013 tone manuscript, which states twice that there is no evidence of stress, contrasts Máíhɨ̃kì explicitly with mixed stress-tone Eastern Tukanoan systems, and settles the older SIL 'accent' notation. Both quotations were confirmed verbatim at the cited pages in held PDFs. No later published version, instrumental study, or competing analysis was found (Michael's 2021 CV; Skilton 2017 downloaded and silent on prosody). Remaining unheld items (Skilton 2014 NM field report; Velie 1975/1976 SIL sketches) are low-priority and unlikely to alter the classification.
